content: The studies conducted by Kilewo et al. (2009) and Marazzi et al. (2009) were cohort studies, while those by Jamieson et al. (2012) and Thomas et al. (2011) were cohort studies embedded within randomized controlled trials. Risk of Bias: The studies by Marazzi et al. (2009), Thistle et al. (2011), and Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012) were downgraded due to potential selection bias, as they lacked detailed feeding histories. Additionally, Jamieson et al. (2012) reported a 20% loss to follow-up, and Thistle et al. (2011) reported a 3% loss to follow-up. Inconsistency: The pooled estimate showed substantial heterogeneity (I² = 83%), leading to a downgrade. HIV-free survival rates varied significantly, ranging from 85% (95% CI: 75%-92%) in Thistle et al. (2011) to 96% (95% CI: 91%-98%) in Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012). Indirectness: The studies were downgraded due to differences in research questions and co-interventions compared to the PICO framework. For example, in Thistle et al. (2011), Marazzi et al. (2009), and Kilewo et al. (2009), the only intervention was antiretroviral therapy (ART). Jamieson et al. (2012) compared HIV-free survival among children whose mothers were on ART, infants on nevirapine (NVP), and a control group, with further subgrouping based on maternal nutritional supplementation. Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012) included ART for all women and prophylaxis for newborns, while Thomas et al. (2011) provided ART to mothers and a single dose of NVP to infants within 72 hours, followed by TMP/SMX from six weeks. Variations in breastfeeding practices, timing of ART initiation, and outcomes of interest were also noted. The study by Tonwe-Gold et al. (2007) was a cohort study, while those by Cohan et al. (2015) and Thakwalakwa et al. were cohort studies embedded within randomized controlled trials. Risk of Bias: Tonwe-Gold et al. (2007) and Thakwalakwa et al. (2011) were downgraded due to insufficient feeding history details. HIV-free survival estimates ranged from 89% (95% CI: 83%-95%) in Tonwe-Gold et al. (2007) to 95% (95% CI: 92%-97%) in Cohan et al. (2015). Indirectness: The studies were downgraded due to differences in research questions and co-interventions. For instance, in Tonwe-Gold et al. (2007), all women were on ART, and infants received single-dose NVP at three days and one week of ZDV syrup. In Cohan et al. (2015), mothers were randomized to receive either efavirenz or lopinavir/ritonavir-based ART, with all receiving trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis. Thakwalakwa et al. randomized infants at six months to receive either milk powder or a ready-to-use food containing peanut paste, skimmed powder, sugar, and vegetable oil. The study by Giuliano et al. (2013) was a retrospective cohort study. ART was discontinued at six months for women with CD4+ counts above 350/mm³ but continued for those with CD4+ counts below 350/mm³. Indirectness: The study was downgraded as its research question did not align with the PICO framework. It assessed HIV-free survival among breastfeeding infants whose mothers were on ART. The studies by Cournil et al. (2015), Coovadia et al. (2012), and Thomas et al. (2011) were cohort studies embedded within randomized controlled trials, while Homsy et al. (2010) and Kilewo et al. (2009) were cohort studies. Risk of Bias: Thomas et al. (2011) was downgraded due to insufficient feeding history details. HIV-free survival rates ranged from 82% (95% CI: 73%-88%) in Homsy et al. (2010) to 96% (95% CI: 94%-99%). Indirectness: The studies were downgraded due to differences in research questions and co-interventions. For example, Cournil et al. (2015) randomized women to receive either triple ARV prophylaxis or short-course ARV. Coovadia et al. (2012) randomized infants to receive extended nevirapine prophylaxis or placebo until six months or breastfeeding cessation. In Thomas et al. (2011), all mothers were on ART, and infants received a single dose of NVP within 72 hours and TMP/SMX from six weeks. Homsy et al. (2010) provided ART to all women, with infants receiving a single dose of NVP within 72 hours, supplemented with AZT syrup. Kilewo et al. (2009) provided ART to all mothers, with infants receiving ZDV + 3TC for one week after birth. The studies by Ngoma et al. (2015), Sagay et al. (2015), and Okafor et al. (2014) were cohort studies. Risk of Bias: Sagay et al. (2015) lacked detailed feeding history, and Okafor et al. (2014) did not specify how HIV-free survival was estimated, leading to a double downgrade. Inconsistency: Substantial heterogeneity was observed (I² = 82%). HIV-free survival ranged from 87% (95% CI: 79%-92%) in Ngoma et al. (2015) to 98% (95% CI: 97%-99%) in Sagay et al. (2015). Indirectness: The studies were downgraded due to differences in research questions and co-interventions. In Ngoma et al. (2015), all women were on ART. In Sagay et al. (2015) and Okafor et al. (2014), HIV-exposed infants received NVP from birth to six weeks, in addition to maternal ART. The studies by Thomas et al. (2011) and Shapiro et al. (2013) were cohort studies embedded within randomized controlled trials. Risk of Bias: Thomas et al. (2011) was downgraded due to insufficient feeding history details. Inconsistency: Substantial heterogeneity was observed (I² = 97%). HIV-free survival ranged from 81%-87% in Thomas et al. (2011) to 94% (95% CI: 92%-96%) in Shapiro et al. (2013). Indirectness: The studies were downgraded as their research questions did not align with the PICO framework. In Shapiro et al. (2013), women received different ART regimens based on CD4 cell counts. In Thomas et al. (2011), all mothers were on ART, and infants received a single dose of NVP within 72 hours and TMP/SMX from six weeks. These findings highlight the variability in study designs, interventions, and outcomes, emphasizing the need for standardized approaches to assess HIV-free survival in the context of maternal ART and infant feeding practices.
